Euronews spoke with TUI's CEO Sebastian Ebel about manure-powered cruise ships, migration, dependence on the US, Artificial Intelligence, and the future of tourism.

TUI Group is regarded as the world's largest integrated tourism group. The firm includes around 460 hotels, 19 cruise ships, five airlines with 125 aircraft and around 1,200 travel agencies with a total of 67,000 employees.

In 2025 the tourism group, headquartered in Hanover, generated revenue of €24.2 billion and an operating profit before interest and taxes of €1.46 billion.

On 9 December the travel group will present its annual figures for 2026.

Euronews spoke to Sebastian Ebel at an economic and innovation summit on the cruise ship "Mein Schiff Flow" in the northern-German city of Kiel.

Euronews: In your view, what should the EU do to stimulate the economy and strengthen competitiveness?

Sebastian Ebel: Bureaucracy is not only the EU's responsibility, national governments are responsible for it as well. I always use Denmark as an example: just as much a member of the EU as Germany, but with a far lower density of regulation. That is perhaps the first point, that we should organise these things that we can regulate ourselves, ourselves and differently and better. Of course in my view the EU apparatus, and I am a convinced European, it is the best peace model we have ever had, needs to be reformed. That includes streamlining it, cutting back regulation and focusing on guard rails.

Euronews: Businesses also complain about labour shortages. Demographic trends in Europe will make the problem even worse. How do you assess this for your sector and for your company?

Sebastian Ebel: I think we face a demographic factor that is challenging. When an age pyramid turns upside down, far fewer people have to support far more older people. That means that, mathematically, we have to work longer, at least those who want to and are able to. And it also means that we need immigration, specifically talented people who can solve the problems we have here. By the way, that is nothing new. I remember the waves in Braunschweig and Wolfsburg of Italians who came to work for VW. I remember people from the Philippines who came here for medical services. The point is that we bring the right people here who can strongly support us in this demographic transition so that it does not backfire on us.

Euronews: Which political and economic framework conditions, the big levers, do we need in Germany and Europe to boost the economy?

Sebastian Ebel: Cutting bureaucracy is the main point for me. If you work here every day as an entrepreneur, you know what you are talking about. Many people are not aware of the obstacles that exist. This also includes taxonomies, that is, a tax system that is simple, it is not always about cuts, but about it being manageable and understandable. Bureaucracy is a key issue.

Euronews: The economy needs affordable energy and stable energy. It has to be available all the time. But can we really supply an industrial country with sustainable energy?

Sebastian Ebel: Of course. Why not? It is the energy that is produced in the most sustainable and most cost effective way, and increasingly it can be produced even better in the future. Today we are failing because we do not have smart grids, so that we can deal with different situations, a lot of energy when it is stormy outside, little energy when it is dark and there is no wind, and cannot get this to the customer.

Euronews: What about storage capacity? That is needed as well.

Sebastian Ebel: There are three things. First, using the energy we have in such a way that when there is a lot of energy it is cheap and when there is little it is expensive, so that self-regulation takes place. The second issue is expanding the grids. That will increasingly be important. And third, working in large interconnected systems.

Euronews: The EU says nuclear energy is climate friendly and can certainly be used. Do you share that view?

Sebastian Ebel: There are new generations of nuclear energy. However, the question is whether there is majority support for it among the population. I have serious doubts whether this is achievable here. In other countries it is, including for example Sweden. I believe this question is not really on the agenda at the moment. Who today would want to build and put into operation a new nuclear power plant in Brokdorf? I think renewable energy can largely cover demand here and at very, very low prices.

Euronews: What is TUI's position on electric mobility? E-ships will never exist.

Sebastian Ebel: We were one of the first groups to say that we would only have company cars that are electric. We decided that two or three years ago and today we are glad we did. We are electrifying our bus fleets, we operate around 1,000 buses with partners worldwide. And we are now slowly beginning to switch to electric buses. We have the topic of hotels, in other words moving away from fossil fuels towards electric energy or geothermal energy to generate power.

Ships have a major advantage, as we have heard today: LNG-powered ships. They should not run on fracked LNG, but on biogas energy from slurry. We can also produce methanol for traditional e-methanol. The big issue remains air travel. Today it is the most demanding area when it comes to making it carbon neutral in the long or medium term.

Euronews: In your opinion, which fuels currently offer the greatest potential, in other words sustainable fuels?

Sebastian Ebel: For ships, I believe very strongly in e-LNG or biogas LNG. And as a second step, methanol. I think this shift in the way the economy sources energy over a defined short period is perfectly feasible and today there is no longer a contradiction between economics and ecology, they go hand in hand. There are, however, some sectors, such as aviation, where there are still real issues that require technological change. Although I was able to learn again today that perhaps we are not that far away from this. When I see that a country like Denmark is completely independent of fossil gas, and that ships here can be fuelled with Danish e-LNG, then this, produced from slurry from livestock farming, water, slurry, straw, is really a model that we could implement in Germany or other European countries in exactly the same way.

Euronews: An important topic is digital sovereignty. Why do we need to become independent of the US players? We could work well with them.

Sebastian Ebel: I think it is important for security reasons, but also for economic reasons. We have just seen again that Starlink was switched off or reduced for Ukraine. I do not want us in Germany to be dependent on the decision of a single man in America as to whether we get a product or not. I believe it is our responsibility, not only for defence but also for economic enterprises. We must not be vulnerable to blackmail. That is one issue. The other is an economic issue. When I look at the margins of our German car industry and the tourism sector in Germany compared with software companies, the balance of power has been suspended. There high margins, here low margins. And I see that where companies have their own software again, negotiations also go better.

Euronews: How are you using AI, artificial intelligence, at TUI?

Sebastian Ebel: We started with flagship projects. We began with optimising route planning and deployment planning. We have used it very extensively in sales to find new distribution channels. And now, through AI factories, as we call them, we are producing software applications, ideally like in a factory

(Editor's note: AI stands for Artificial Intelligence, German "Künstliche Intelligenz").

Euronews: Tourism, a brief look back. How has 2026 been for TUI so far?

Sebastian Ebel: 2026 was another difficult year. On top of all the economic developments, the war in the east and the challenges in the west, the war involving Iran was added. We had a one off effect because ships were held there and for two or three months we saw a very sharp slowdown in bookings, with long haul travel also heavily affected. Against this backdrop we have performed very, very well. We did not have to withdraw the guidance (Editor's note: the official forecast by the management for future business development) that we issued three months ago. The resilience that we as TUI have shown is something not everyone would have credited us with.

Euronews: What are the trend destinations of the future, if we look a bit ahead?

Sebastian Ebel: Cruises will remain strong. I would say everything related to experiences will grow even more. Whether it is a theme park, the best diving spot or a Dine&Wine course. Market segmentation will become more intense. And then, perhaps as the overarching effect, many people have a fixed budget, especially in economically challenging times. Offering something for this budget, for a single mother or father with one child or for grandparents with their grandchildren, that is one of our main tasks.

Euronews: Overtourism is always an issue. Cruise ships are viewed very critically as well. But what positive effects does tourism have?

Sebastian Ebel: Tourism is seen as extremely positive in the destinations. What we often do here is focus on what happens at two demonstrations in Mallorca. Worldwide, tourism is seen very, very positively. And there are regions, also in Germany by the way, that suffer from overtourism. In such cases it is up to governments to say what kind of tourism they want. Because if the people on the ground are not happy, then the customers are not either.

And the point is that we are told what kind of tourism is wanted. The main point of criticism is often transport and, in particular, housing. Housing is the overriding issue when people still live at home at 25 because they can no longer afford a flat, or houses are always bought by foreigners at higher prices. And there I would recommend that those responsible introduce regulation so that people get the right kind of tourism and in the right quantity.

Euronews: If you could make three or four decisions, if you were the President of the Commission or the German Chancellor, what are the three or four most important decisions where you would say: we have to take these now, otherwise time will run out on us?

Sebastian Ebel: Massive cutting of bureaucracy. Bringing energy prices down to an acceptable level, launching an education offensive for talent, in other words upgrading schools and universities, and making sure that investment pays off again.

Euronews: Thank you very much for the interview.

Sebastian Ebel: My pleasure.

Euronews Next spoke to Jen Wong about the threat of AI to the open internet and the importance of human connection on the platform.

In the 21 years since its founding, Reddit has played host to some of the strangest, most niche corners of the internet — from knitting groups to discussions about romantic relationships between humans and artificial intelligence.

AI has dramatically transformed the internet for Reddit users in those two-plus decades. Even so, the technology still has the potential to deepen the value of human conversation on the platform, as it “has no inherent taste… and doesn’t know anything,” Reddit’s chief operating officer, Jen Wong, told Euronews Next on the sidelines of Web Summit 2026 earlier this month.

She described Reddit as "the taste layer of the internet", arguing that AI models will always need human communities to understand new products, culture and ways of speaking.

“Reddit — it's fun, it's a place to build together, it's a place where there's something different about getting advice from a group of different people versus having it synthesised by an AI agent,” she said.

Reddit operates on the basis of individually themed groups called subreddits. Users can post links and create their own rules, such as a ban on overt self-promotion or guidelines around authenticity. There are also human moderators who can report extremist or violent behaviour on the platform.

Reddit users increased to 443.8 million weekly active users as of the third quarter of 2025, up from 365.4 million during the same period a year prior. In October, the company said its net income had soared more than 74% on an annual basis in the third quarter of this year.

Still, Wong acknowledged that AI search is harming Reddit's traffic. Search referrals declined in the company's most recently reported quarter, she said, adding that AI search is "not a material traffic driver" in the way traditional blue links were.

Demand for the platform, though, has not disappeared. Reddit remains a top-15 search term, but AI products make it harder for people to reach it. Reddit’s focus now, Wong said, is on logged-in users and those on its application, while also driving traffic to the platform directly.

‘The arms race’

In the interview, Wong argued that AI search is partly to blame for making the internet more closed and siloed than it was 20 years ago.

“I think we have been real believers and beneficiaries of what was an open internet but I think that's changed. I think the internet is not as open,” she said.

Wong also faulted AI for "intensive data stealing and abuse and scraping", which she said has made publishers more guarded.

Reddit currently has partnerships with OpenAI and Google for data sharing. Rather than feeding AI with user content, Wong said the partnerships allow for the company to “lay down guardrails on how our data is being used”.

Data scraping is against Reddit’s terms of service and Wong said it has built-in defences against it. But she acknowledged that “over time that will be an arms race, frankly”. Amid a wave of AI agents and assistants, it could become increasingly difficult to ensure that Reddit users are, indeed, human.

Reddit's approach to AI agents has been to create "clear, sanctioned avenues" for them so their activity is transparent. Bots are acceptable, she said, if they are labelled, and some, such as news feed bots, could even be useful.

When asked about criticism that AI models trained on Reddit data inherit bias, particularly against women, Wong defended the platform as now being "one of the most balanced" on diversity of opinion.

Wong added that while the site's early audience skewed male and tech-oriented, Reddit is now "very gender balanced," with Gen Z women its fastest-growing demographic in some countries, including the United Kingdom.

Reddit in the future

Looking ahead, Wong predicted that over the next five years AI agents will transform Reddit’s business across the board, from user experience to advertising buying. But she insisted the company will maintain its core principles.

“When it seems like everyone's zigging and you're zagging,” she said, “believing in communities, moderation, privacy and anonymity has served us really well.”

Wong added that Reddit’s commitment to human connection would ultimately allow it to adapt to a new technological reality. “When people come together, as we see in real life, it is an incredible trove of lived experience and knowledge,” she said.

From hotels with dedicated gaming rooms to real-life destinations featured in blockbuster titles, video games are increasingly influencing holiday plans. New data reveals a surge in searches for gaming-themed stays, with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI helping fuel the trend.

After years of waiting, video game fans have been celebrating the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, with stories of people locking themselves away for days at a time to play the game going viral.

Now, it seems as if the long-awaited launch is inspiring travel.

New research – called “Get a Room” – from Hotels.com shows that travellers are on the hunt for gaming-inspired stays, which range from escapes which feel familiar to long-time players to immersive hotel stays designed for marathon gaming sessions.

It comes after experts said so-called “gami-vacations” would be one of the top trends for 2026, with gamers travelling to real-life locations featured in titles such as Ghost of Tsushima, Assassin’s Creed, and God of War. Tourism boards have also been partnering with game developers to tap into the trend.

It certainly seems to be paying off. The Hotels.com data reveals that global searches for properties with gaming rooms have surged by 220% from September to November 2026, while searches for hotels offering room service grew by 65% over the same period, suggesting people are taking trips in order to switch off and settle into their own virtual world.

Nostalgic destinations and gaming-ready hotels

In terms of trending destinations, it’s nostalgia which features the most. The data revealed that searches for Miami have jumped 70% year-over-year, while searches for Panama City Beach are up 130%. Both cities inspired the fictional “Vice City”, where GTA VI is set. It seems as if people are keen to experience neon-lit streets and palm-lined boulevards for themselves – even if they’re staying inside playing the game.

Some hotels are already getting involved with the trend, offering dedicated gaming facilities for guests who want to fit in a few sessions between sightseeing.

In Germany’s capital, the nhow Berlin hotel has purpose-built gaming rooms with high-spec equipment and console setups, while Sweden's Steam Hotel has a dedicated gaming suite designed for playing with friends.

Gaming getaways aren't just limited to city breaks, either. The Kandima Maldives resort has its own PlaySpace, complete with gaming facilities and social areas where guests can switch between virtual adventures and a spot of island relaxation.

In 2027, the trend will go one step further. A new Minecraft World Hotel is set to open near London next year, giving fans the chance to sleep inside the world of the best-selling video game of all time.

Gami-vacations go up a gear

It’s not just GTA and hotels which are part of the trend – gaming holidays, or “gami-vacations”, are becoming an increasingly popular way to travel, too.

Fans are increasingly heading to real-life locations featured in their favourite video games, seeking out experiences inspired by virtual adventures or travelling to major gaming conventions.

The trend is being driven by the popularity of titles such as Ghost of Tsushima and Assassin's Creed, alongside a growing appetite for hobby-based travel. Travellers are choosing to immerse themselves in places connected to their interests and bring their favourite fictional worlds into real life.

There are plenty of destinations to choose from. Norway's Jotunheimen mountains feature in God of War, while Scotland provides the backdrop for parts of Assassin's Creed.

Fans of Ghost of Tsushima can visit Tsushima Island in Japan, while Montana in the US is associated with Far Cry 5 and offers the chance to explore the spectacular landscapes of Glacier National Park.

Some trips take the gaming experience a step further, with apps offering missions, quests, challenges, rewards and badges, turning sightseeing into something resembling a real-life game.

Others plan their holidays around major gaming events and conventions, including Germany's Gamescom and Paris Games Week.

Tourism boards are also waking up to the potential of gaming tourism, with some partnering directly with developers to put their destinations on the map. Czechia, for example, has worked with the creators of Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 to promote locations featured in the game.

Any pollution entering the water could have a possible impact on Mediterranean seagrasses that absorb substantial quantities of climate-heating carbon dioxide.

Spanish authorities are scrambling to contain any damage to its "vulnerable" Mediterranean waters following a huge oil spill.

On Thursday (26 November), a tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel sank off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one dead.

The Maltese-flagged Med Emre was travelling from the southern port of Algeciras to Barcelona when it sank in the early hours of the morning. 17 crew members were rescued but one was later confirmed dead in hospital.

According to maritime data tracking firm Kpler, the vessel was transporting around 66,000 barrels of refined products.

It is currently unclear what caused the sinking.

A government mechanism designed for marine pollution events had been activated, "but this does not presuppose that pollution has been detected on the coast", Spanish government sources told news agency AFP.

A boat and a plane belonging to Spanish maritime rescue service Salvamento Maritimo had been sent to assess the possible environmental damage, the Balearic emergency services added.

The Civil Protection authority had requested the activation of the European Union's Earth monitoring system Copernicus to obtain images of the area, said the government sources.

'Amplified' potential for pollution

Maritime security expert Emilio Rodriguez Diaz from the University of Cadiz told local news that the area affected by the oil spill was "particularly vulnerable".

Any pollution entering the water could have a possible impact on tourism and on Mediterranean seagrasses that absorb substantial quantities of climate-heating carbon dioxide.

Mediterranean seagrass acts as a major blue carbon sink, trapping carbon in deep rhizome and sediment layers while oxygenating coastal waters - but warming waters from climate change is already fuelling their demise.

The area also includes spaces protected by the European Union's Natura 2000 network and hosts the critically endangered Balearic Shearwater, says SEOBirdLife.

"Contact with the fuel may alter the impermeability and the thermal insulation of the birds' plumage, causing heat loss and hypothermia," the NGO warned.

Marine conservation group Oceana noted that the time of year was "key" for migratory species, including turtles, sharks, red tuna, pilot whales and the striped dolphin.

Oil spills are one of the most concerning sources of marine pollution as they're difficult to clean up and can last for a long time.

"They can severely pollute marine and coastal habitats, causing damage to the natural environment and the economy," says the European Environment Agency.

"The Mediterranean Sea’s highly industrialised nature, characterised by the many extensive ports, refineries and petrochemical plants along its coastlines, amplifies the potential for pollution incidents."

Spain's worst oil spill

But Diaz downplayed comparisons to the 2002 Prestige oil disaster, Spain's worst environmental accident so far.

That spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of fuel and blackened thousands of kilometres of Atlantic coastline, affecting Spain, Portugal and France.

The Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood", he said.

"It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment."

In December 2024, a US-sanctioned Russian cargo ship sank in international waters off Spain's southern Mediterranean coast with 16 people on board -- two of whom were never found.

A Spanish government letter to parliament earlier this year revealed the ship was transporting "components of two nuclear reactors similar to those used by submarines".

The vessel's owner, a company that belongs to the Russian defence ministry, denounced at the time "a targeted terrorist attack", without providing evidence.

The value of the pledge is unknown. It depends on the share price, but also on how many Trump Accounts are eligible for this offer.

To receive shares through the programme, parents or guardians must claim and activate their child's Trump Account. The US government provides a one-off $1,000 (€914) contribution for eligible US citizens born from 2025 through 2028.

The money is generally invested in low-cost funds that track the US stock market, and withdrawals are usually restricted until the year the child turns 18.

The White House said nearly 70 million accounts had been created by October. It is unclear how many have been activated.

The US Federal Communications Commission authorised Elon Musk's rocket company to create a data centre constellation to power AI on earth.

The Trump administration on Wednesday gave Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX the green light to deploy one million satellites that it said would create data centres in space, as governments increasingly look to alternative means to power artificial intelligence.

The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) lauded its authorisation as a historic first amid the AI race. It said that SpaceX's one million "orbital compute modules" — forming a data centre constellation called Starmind — would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth.

"America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move "opens a bold new frontier".

A lengthier authorisation order published by the FCC noted that SpaceX must deploy at least "one authorised space station" by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media.

In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules and that deploying the satellites "serves the public interest". But it acknowledged that it had received a “substantial number” of public comments leading up to its authorisation on Wednesday, including petitions to deny SpaceX's request.

The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centres in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns like atmospheric pollution caused by launches and reentries.

Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun’s energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth, as well as the resources like water needed to cool them.

European data centres in space?

The European Union is also exploring how to construct data centres in space.

The European Commission’s 16-month, €2 million Horizon Europe ASCEND feasibility study, which was conducted by an industry-led research consortium, found that building solar-powered data centres in orbit is technically and economically viable. It proposed an initial 10 MW deployment by 2036 scaling to 1 GW by 2050.

A review by the European Parliament of the ASCEND proposal in April noted that data centres in space could ease constraints on terrestrial centres, including their high electrical demands. But it also noted that the "main barrier is economic, rather than technical, with future launch costs a key determinant".

Meanwhile, China launched an initial cluster of 12 AI computing satellites in May 2025 as the first phase of its planned 2,800-satellite "Three-Body Computing Constellation" led by ADA Space and Zhejiang Lab.

One in three 16- to 24-year-olds have never had sex, up from one in five in 2010.

Young people in Britain are having less sex than in the past, but many are sending or receiving sexual images and watching pornography, a large new study has found.

“Britain’s sex lives are changing. While most adults are having sex, people are having sex less often and more young people have never had sex,” said Soazig Clifton, an epidemiologist at University College London and academic director for the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (NATSAL).

"There is also a higher proportion of people reporting same-sex experiences, and online sexual activity is now part of everyday life for many," Clifton said.

The study, which was published in The Lancet, found that most people in Britain aged 16 to 59 were sexually active, with a median of five lifetime partners. Around two-thirds reported having had one sexual partner in the past year, while women had sex an average of once a month and men twice a month.

The decline is particularly pronounced among younger generations. Among 16- to 24-year-olds, the proportion who said they had never had sex has risen to one in three, compared with one in five in 2010.

Overall, the frequency of sexual activity has declined among people under 45, falling to about twice a month, compared with four times a month in 1990.

The fourth edition of the NATSAL study, which has conducted regular surveys since 1990, is based on responses from 6,719 people aged 16 to 59.

Conducted between 2022 and 2024, the research noted similar trends in other industrialised countries.

Despite the decline in in-person sexual activity, online sexual behaviours are widespread, particularly among younger age groups.

Nearly half of 16- to 24-year-olds said they had sent or received sexual images on their phones in the previous year: 47.1% of young women and 43.5% of young men. The practice was less common among older age groups.

Pornography consumption was also widespread among people under 35. Around half of young women reported having watched pornography, compared with nearly nine in 10 young men.

The researchers found "widespread engagement with pornography and sexting across age groups and genders," a pattern also observed in other countries.

"Together with declines in in-person sex, this might signal a shift away from partnered physical intimacy, towards more solo and online sexual behaviour."

The study also found "increased diversity in the gender of partners" across all age groups.

"Sexual behaviour is a fundamental part of the human experience and changes in tandem with wider social changes," the researchers said.

They stressed that these societal shifts "carry significant implications for sexual and mental health and public health practice".

"We might be tempted to link the decrease in sexual frequency and the increase in childlessness, but we'd be wrong," said Kaye Wellings, professor of sexual and reproductive health research at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.

"People who want to conceive have sex often enough to make sure they do. To understand these trends, we need to look at a complex range of features of the society we now live in," added Wellings, who was not involved in the study.

The researchers said the reasons behind these changes are not yet well understood. However, they pointed to broader societal developments that may have played a role, including rising rates of common mental health conditions, declining alcohol consumption and increasingly online lifestyles.

The United Kingdom reportedly sent a Sri Lankan refugee who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, where he committed suicide, as part of an undisclosed deal, according to a BBC investigation.

The man, 35-year-old Kishanth Peramalya, had no connection to the southern African country.

He had left India in 2021 in an attempt to seek asylum in Canada. The Royal Navy rescued him and dozens of other Sri Lankan asylum seekers while their boat sailed in the Indian Ocean, the BBC reported. They were sent to Diego Garcia, an island in the British Indian Ocean Territory that serves as a UK-US military base.

The group of 61 asylum seekers stayed on the island for three years. In 2024, a report from the United Nations refugee agency denounced their detention conditions and said they should be urgently relocated.

By the end of 2024, most of the refugees were allowed to enter the UK but not Peramalya. During his detention, he had committed several crimes and had been convicted of four counts of sexual assault, according to the BBC.

The UK refused to welcome Peramalya due to his criminal convictions but acknowledged he could not return to Sri Lanka, where he had been tortured and sexual assaulted by military officers as a teenager. A UK court upheld the government's decision not to admit him to the country, the BBC said.

In March 2026, the Maldives reportedly agreed to take Peramalya for 30 days. He was then transferred to Eswatini, where his already fragile mental health further deteriotated. He committed suicide on September 13.

The BBC said Peramalya's tranfer to Eswatini was the subject of a draft deal between the UK and Eswatini.

According to the document, which Africanews has not seen, the UK government had agreed to cover the costs of Peramalya's permanent resettlement during three years. The deal was not disclosed to the UK Parliament. Peramalya's sister told the BBC that his family had been unaware that his relocation to Eswatini would be permanent.

"The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances,” Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, told the Guardian.

The UK did not specify why it had chosen to deport Peramalya to Eswatini. Since 2025, Eswatini has accepted several third-country deportees from the United States, a move that has drawn criticism in the southern African country.

"Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people," a spokesperson for the UK government told the BBC. "That includes taking steps to ensure high-harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK."

The rollout in Zambia is part of a plan to ensure people in lower-income countries can access the breakthrough HIV prevention drug.

The first shipments of a generic version of a twice-a-year HIV-prevention shot arrived on Wednesday in Zambia, and additional deliveries are expected in Uganda in the coming days.

The medication is called lenacapavir and is expected to cost $40 (€36) a year per person. It will eventually be available in 120 countries. The injectable form of pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, is nearly 100% effective at preventing an HIV infection and much more convenient than daily preventive pills that are available now.

“With demand for the injection far outstripping supply, the arrival of generics marks a major step towards making this breakthrough prevention option more widely available and affordable in low- and middle-income countries,” said Tenu Avafia, deputy executive director of Unitaid, a global health agency.

The medications are part of a shipment by the Global Fund, a worldwide partnership to defeat AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria. After going through a clearance process in Zambia, the medications are expected to be used within the next three weeks.

In 2025, the European Commission and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved brand-name lenacapavir, which is made by Gilead Sciences. The FDA approved the generic shot earlier this month, though it cannot be sold in the United States because it is still protected by Gilead’s patent.

Gilead established royalty-free licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable greater production of lenacapavir. Those voluntary licenses cover a specific set of countries in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and Latin America.

Gilead officials said the company signed the licenses months before regulatory approval to ensure an early generic supply, and collaborated closely with generic manufacturers and global health partners.

The FDA-approved generic was developed by India-based Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories under an agreement brokered by Unitaid and its partners, which sought to accelerate development and make the drug available at an affordable price.

“Access is a priority because we know that breakthroughs like lenacapavir only matter when they reach the people who need them most,” Daniel O’Day, Gilead’s chairman and CEO, said in a press release.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV and 570,000 died from HIV-related causes last year.

“We have an unprecedented opportunity to reach millions more people at risk of HIV,” Peter Sands, executive director of the Global Fund, said in a press release. “This is how we bring the goal of ending AIDS within reach.”

The ongoing outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.

Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire (CRP) rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometres north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.

CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.

Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization’s Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

The latest incident comes despite Denmark upgrading its cybersecurity systems after an earlier breach exposed data linked to millions of people.

Hackers broke into Denmark's national registry and accessed the personal information of 11,000 people, the Danish government said on Thursday, two months after another huge data hack.

Danish authorities said they had updated and modernised their security systems since the previous attack in early October, when the data of 8.8 million people was illegally accessed.

Despite that, "the administration of the Civil Registration System (CPR) has discovered a new security breach," the digital affairs ministry said.

"Unauthorised third parties have accessed the CPR data of 11,000 people."

It added: "The incident was stopped thanks to a new technical monitoring system for consultations, introduced after the first incident."

Neither the perpetrators of the latest breach nor those behind the October hack have been identified yet.

But in October an unidentified person contacted Danish newspaper Politiken in English via an encrypted messaging service and claimed responsibility for that breach.

The supposed hacker said they had found an entry point into the register within a few hours by using the login credentials of a former employee of a small Danish company.

They said the employee's password was 123456.

"The hacker says there were no security measures, such as two-factor verification, and that he was therefore able to start carrying out searches in the CPR register," Politiken wrote at the time.

The individual said they made a total of 14,919,352 queries in the database over a 10-day period.

These consisted of checking whether a specific identification number existed.

If it did, the register would provide the name, address, date of birth, gender, date of last move and marital status of the person concerned.

The suspected hacker recorded all the data but told the newspaper they had "no idea how it could be used" and did not intend to sell or disclose it.

In September, the Civil Security Agency raised the threat level for cyberattacks against Denmark to "high".

Heat pumps are becoming increasingly popular amid spiralling gas prices, but can the green technology survive a freezing winter?

Leaders have been urged to make it easier to install heat pumps in every building across Europe, as the US-led war on Iran continues to send gas prices soaring.

There are currently an estimated 30 million residential heat pumps installed on the continent, with around three million added in 2025. While this may sound like a significant increase, it is a million below the four million target set out by the European Commission.

A new analysis from the European Heat Pump Association (EHPA) found that fitting heat pumps in every building and “compatible industrial process” – powered by renewables like solar and wind – would avoid around 600 million tonnes (Mt) of CO2.

To put that into perspective, this is more than the annual emissions of Germany, the bloc’s biggest economy, or the 17 smallest EU countries combined.

But as Europe faces a potentially freezing winter, can heat pumps withstand the cold?

How do heat pumps work?

Heat pumps capture energy from air, water or the ground and turn it into heat or cold air – rather than burning fossil fuels on-site.

Think of it like a refrigerator but in reverse: heat pumps use a liquid chemical that turns into a hot gas through compression, which is then released into your central heating and hot water tank.

For every one kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity they consume, heat pumps typically deliver three to four kWh of heat. It is this efficiency that means they can run in the winter for a little as €2.20 per day.

Do heat pumps work in cold weather?

Contrary to popular myths, modern heat pumps can still extract heat from the air even in low temperatures.

“The key is the refrigerant: a special chemical that can boil even at very low temperatures,” explains UK energy firm Octopus Energy. “That means even when it feels cold outside to you and me (say -20°C), the air temperature is still hot enough to boil the refrigerant in your heat pump.

“That boiling action soaks up a bunch of heat energy. Then through the magic of valves and a compressor, the refrigerant temperature soars up to 65°C and gives up its heat to your radiator water. Then the cycle repeats.”

Of course, lower temperatures mean that the heat pump has to work harder, but experts say a modern heat pump can still perform at three times more efficiency than a traditional gas boiler during freezing conditions.

It’s therefore no surprise that Norway, Finland and Sweden, some of Europe’s coldest countries, have some of the highest heat pump installations in the continent.

According to EHPA, more than half the households in these countries already have a heat pump – while traditionally warmer countries like Spain and Portugal lag behind.

Can heat pumps work in old buildings?

Another common myth is that heat pumps are solely reserved for new build homes, with previous reports claiming the green technology would be impractical for more than half (54 per cent) of British households due to factors such as poor insulation and limited space.

However, The Fraunhofer Society, Europe’s largest application-oriented research organisation, states that heat pumps outperform gas boilers even in buildings more than 100 years old.

In a 2019 study, buildings between 15 and 150 years old that had been partially or fully refurbished with energy-saving measures, including a heat pump being installed, were analysed.

Researchers found that air-source heat pumps achieved an average seasonal performance rating of 3.1, meaning they’re more than three times more efficient than a gas boiler.

Veterans say they were effectively used as test subjects, with some exposed to radioactive fallout without adequate protection.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced an independent inquiry into the impact of Britain’s Cold War nuclear weapons tests on military veterans and their families.

In a statement, the prime minister said: "Nuclear test veterans and their families have waited too long for the truth, and that’s exactly what the independent panel will establish."

Around 22,000 British service personnel witnessed nuclear tests in the Indian and Pacific oceans between 1952 and 1967. Many of those affected say they felt they were used as test subjects, with some exposed to radioactive fallout without adequate protection.

Veterans and their families have campaigned for recognition and compensation for around 40 years, linking the tests to illnesses affecting both participants and, in some cases, their children.

Campaigners met the prime minister at an event at 10 Downing Street. It came a day after the BBC aired a special edition of Newsnight on Tuesday, in which some surviving veterans shared their experiences.

Britain's nuclear tests

The UK's first atmospheric atomic test took place on 3 October 1952, when a plutonium implosion device was detonated near the Montebello Islands off Western Australia.

Dozens more nuclear explosions were carried out by the UK in Australia and Pacific territories, including Kiritimati, formerly known as Christmas Island.

Campaigners say many military personnel were exposed to nuclear fallout after being ordered to fly through mushroom clouds or witness explosions without protective equipment.

Unlike the United States and France, the UK has no dedicated compensation scheme for nuclear test veterans.

Britain's Ministry of Defence has said there was no evidence that Britain’s nuclear tests had caused increased health risks, citing four studies as well as research by Brunel University in 2022.

However, veterans and campaigners have accused the MoD of withholding complete medical records, including blood and urine test results, which they argue could help establish a link between radiation exposure and illness later in life.

The MoD released some official documents in July 2026, but said some records may have been inadvertently destroyed three years earlier.

An independent panel will take on the investigation

The British government says the panel will be modelled on the Hillsborough Independent Panel, rather than being a conventional statutory public inquiry. It says this should allow for a faster, more collaborative process, with veterans and their families closely involved.

The government says the panel's terms of reference are likely to include the conditions servicemen were exposed to, what the state knew and when, advice given to ministers and statements made to Parliament, as well as how veterans and their health concerns were handled.

The panel is expected to deliver an interim report by 3 October 2027, the 75th anniversary of Britain's first nuclear weapons test.

Andy Burnham said his government would also pursue memorialisation, education and research alongside the inquiry, rather than waiting for its final conclusions.

A national memorial service is being planned for 3 October 2027.

The EU is preparing a voluntary agreement to accelerate data centre expansion as it seeks to triple capacity within five to seven years, despite growing concerns about electricity consumption and pressure on power grids.

A leaked European Commission draft accessed by Euronews reveals that the EU wants national governments, operators and energy companies to agree on measures to make new data centres easier to build and connect to electricity networks.

But rather than imposing binding sustainability requirements, the Commission is proposing a framework countries can adapt to their needs.

The document, "EU model for tripartite agreements on the sustainable integration of data centres into the energy system", describes the proposed commitments as a "toolbox rather than a single integrated package that needs to be adopted as such".

Countries could pick and choose measures covering grid access, renewable energy, storage, flexibility and the reuse of excess heat from data centres to warm buildings. Crucially, the draft states that "participation in local tripartite agreements is voluntary" and that the commitments "do not create any legal obligations for the signatory parties".

In parallel, Brussels is developing separate rules and standards to improve data centres' sustainability, raising questions about their compatibility with voluntary industry participation.

Europe's growing appetite for data centres

Data centres are facilities packed with servers that store, process and transmit digital information. They power everything from online banking and cloud services to AI, which demands huge computing capacity.

The leaked draft puts the EU's installed data centre capacity at approximately 12 gigawatts in 2025. According to International Energy Agency estimates, capacity stood at around 52 gigawatts in the US and 28 gigawatts in China that year.

The Commission sees expanding capacity as key to digital sovereignty. But MEP Benedetta Scuderi questioned whether this would strengthen Europe's autonomy, particularly if new infrastructure is developed by American technology companies.

"We know that we have very scarce resources for building data centres: energy, water and land. We need to be sure that what we build is what we need, that we don't go beyond that, that these data centres are not oversized or unnecessarily large-scale, and that they support our digital sovereignty. We cannot sell out our natural resources to American Big Tech because that would be of no benefit to us."

Data centres require huge supplies of electricity and cooling systems that can consume vast amounts of water. According to the Commission's draft, they already account for around 2.5% of EU electricity consumption, while their concentration near major hubs is increasing pressure on local grids.

That challenges Europe's energy transition, which also requires electricity for transport, buildings and industrial decarbonisation.

The draft's plans for centres and member states

The Commission is trying to balance these priorities through several energy and digital policy initiatives, including the Cloud and AI Development Act. Existing EU environmental and energy-efficiency rules already require data centres to report on sustainability, including energy efficiency and water use.

The leaked draft also mentions a common EU sustainability rating scheme to make facilities' environmental performance easier to compare. It proposes a collaborative approach through tripartite agreements, bringing together public authorities, data centre operators and energy companies to negotiate arrangements for individual projects or broader national and regional development plans.

According to the draft, the aim is to support "faster rollout of data centre projects, improve their visibility, improve local acceptance, and add value to the energy system and the community".

For member states, this could mean designating areas for new data centres based on grid capacity, environmental factors and opportunities to reuse excess heat. Authorities would also be encouraged to coordinate electricity, heating and digital infrastructure planning, streamline grid connections and prevent speculative projects from hogging scarce capacity. The draft suggests checking whether projects have permits, financing and sufficient technical readiness before granting grid access.

Data centre operators would share electricity demand forecasts and project updates with grid operators and consider flexible connection agreements. These could speed up grid access in exchange for limiting electricity consumption at certain times. Operators would also be encouraged to invest in clean power, sign long-term power purchase agreements and shift computing workloads to periods when electricity is more readily available.

Waste heat is another major focus, as heat generated by servers could be recovered to warm homes, schools and hospitals through district heating networks. The draft encourages operators to publish heat-reuse readiness plans, explore connections to local heating networks and negotiate long-term commercial deals where feasible. Governments could help through infrastructure planning, heat purchase agreements for public buildings and funding to cover upfront costs.

Voluntary commitments versus environmental ambitions

The proposed framework does not require every new facility to finance enough additional renewable energy to cover its consumption. Instead, it proposes that member states "explore options for pursuing the time matching of clean energy supply" with data centre demand, leaving the intervals, shares and implementation timelines to national authorities.

Scuderi warned of the consequences of increasing electricity demand in already strained energy systems.

"If you put a huge increase in electricity demand on an already pressured electricity system, what will happen is that we will have a collapse of the system. We will have a huge increase in prices, and we will not know where to get electricity for things that are strategic, such as industry and households.

"When you are asking for a certain number of megawatts for a data centre, we need to know where we're getting this electricity. This needs to come mostly from renewable energy.

"We need to require data centres to produce a certain amount of renewable energy, and the increase in the number of data centres needs to be sustainable in terms of electricity production, without an increase in emissions and without relying on fossil fuel-based electricity production."

While the EU's Energy Efficiency Directive already contains requirements for assessing waste-heat recovery opportunities, the draft's additional commitments would remain voluntary.

It also allows for commercial and technical constraints: where no heat recovery agreement is reached, operators could proceed with facilities designed to accommodate future heat exports. The framework would encourage earlier planning and cooperation without guaranteeing that recoverable heat will reach nearby communities.

While the document presents sustainability as a central objective, it also explicitly seeks to make data centre development faster and more predictable.

The Commission's role

Despite the voluntary nature of the agreements, the Commission plans to retain a central coordinating role, having developed the model with input from authorities in 18 member states and 14 industry associations representing data centres, electricity networks, renewables and storage.

The first local agreements could begin in 2027, potentially alongside data centre acceleration zones under the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act. Brussels would monitor progress annually until at least 2035, share best practices and regularly update the Energy Council and, where appropriate, the European Parliament.

Duran Duran members also shared individual statements on their website, with frontman Simon Le Bon remembering “the blond bombshell, firebrand teenager I met in 1980″.

“He’s the kid from the Northeast who can really play guitar,” he recalled. “If you like, he can play it like Mick Ronson, or he can play it like Jimmy Page, he can even play rinky-dink rhythm like Nile Rodgers. Taylor published his memoir "Wild Boy: My Life In Duran Duran" in 2008.

He is survived by his wife Tracey Wilson, and their four children Andrew, Georgina, Bethany and Isabella.

KNF's approval completes the authorisation process for the Commerzbank deal. Governance, the German public stake and the next stages of the offer still need to be defined.

UniCredit has also obtained the final regulatory clearance needed to press ahead with the public takeover and exchange offer for Commerzbank. On 26 November the Polish financial supervisory authority (KNF) approved the transaction, completing the approval process required for the acquisition of the German bank. The green light from Warsaw was the last missing piece after authorisations from the European Commission and the US Federal Reserve.

The Polish approval specifically concerns the indirect change of control of Commerzbank's operations in Poland, including mBank, in which the German group holds 69.1 per cent. It is one of the country's main banking institutions, with around 5.9 million customers, and is also active in mortgages, investment and payments.

KNF authorisation was necessary because the acquisition of Commerzbank also entails UniCredit taking control of its Polish subsidiaries. Banking rules stipulate that a change of control of the parent company must be reviewed by the supervisory authorities also with regard to qualified indirect holdings in its subsidiaries.

The approval process and the agreement with Berlin

The Polish green light comes after that of the European Commission, which on 16 November cleared the deal unconditionally from a competition standpoint. Brussels assessed the impact of integrating Commerzbank and HypoVereinsbank (HVB), UniCredit's German subsidiary, and ruled out negative effects on the market. Authorisation from the Federal Reserve was granted in the same period.

On the political front, a decisive step was the agreement reached in mid-November between UniCredit's chief executive, Andrea Orcel, and the German government. To overcome Berlin's resistance, the Italian group made eight binding commitments regarding the bank's industrial and employment prospects and the preservation of a strong presence in Germany.

The guarantees include the central role of Frankfurt as the base for German operations, the retention of Commerzbank's stock market listing and its legal form as a German joint-stock company. UniCredit has also pledged to ensure adequate representation of Commerzbank and HypoVereinsbank on the group's executive committee and to propose the appointment of German nationals to its own board of directors when it is renewed in 2027.

The other commitments concern support for German small and medium-sized enterprises, the so-called Mittelstand, through UniCredit's international network, the appropriate allocation of capital and decision-making autonomy for operations in Germany. Investment in Frankfurt is also planned in training, digital technologies and artificial intelligence, along with continued dialogue with trade unions and protection of existing agreements for employees.

The issue of the German state's stake

The question of the state's stake in Commerzbank remains open. The German government holds about 13.3 per cent of the share capital through the SoFFin stabilisation fund and had already announced in June that it would not take part in UniCredit's offer by tendering its shares.

Berlin has not so far announced an immediate sale of its stake. The state's presence in the shareholding structure is also a way to monitor developments in the transaction closely and to verify that UniCredit honours its commitments, particularly on governance, employment and Germany's role in the group's activities.

Next steps

With the completion of regulatory approvals, the deal can now move on to the next stages of implementation. The crediting of the new shares to the custodian banks is scheduled to take place by 7 December 2026.

UniCredit has also asked Commerzbank to call an extraordinary general meeting to elect a new board of directors. This step is part of the process of defining the future governance of the German bank.

For UniCredit, the transaction implies an estimated capital absorption of between 200 and 225 basis points of CET1, the main indicator of a bank's capital strength, in return for a significant expected contribution to the group's profits.

Greece is opening 20 new day centres for people with Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia.

Greece's Ministry of Health is moving ahead with plans to launch specialised services for people with Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.

It will create and operate 20 new day centres for comprehensive mental health care, which will be supported by mobile units and will provide free services to citizens across the country.

The new facilities are part of the plan to reform psychiatric services and implement Greece's national dementia strategy. Strengthening community care and ensuring equal access to specialised services are key goals.

"With the 20 new day centres, we are building a coherent care network for dementia across the country, with an emphasis on community care, continuity of therapeutic support and the active involvement of the family," said Dimitris Vartzopoulos, Greece's deputy minister of health.

The 20 new centres will provide comprehensive, personalised care, tailored to the needs and stage of the illness of each patient. The aim of these programmes is to preserve the cognitive and functional abilities of people with dementia, strengthen their autonomy and improve their daily functioning.

They also aim to prevent or delay the worsening of symptoms, reduce social isolation and avoid early institutionalisation. The extended opening hours of the facilities are expected to make it easier for patients and their families to access the services.

Meanwhile, the mobile units will provide home care, particularly in cases where it is difficult or impossible for patients to travel to the centres.

The new facilities will also offer support for family carers, who shoulder much of the day-to-day care of people with dementia. They can access counselling services, psychological support and training programmes to help them manage caregiving demands.

The development of these services is particularly important, as dementia affects not only those who are ill, but also their family and social environment. The growing need for care, combined with an ageing population, makes it necessary to create facilities that provide stable, specialised and accessible support.

"Dementia does not concern only the person who is ill, but also their family, their carers and society as a whole," Vartzopoulos said. "The state must stand by them, with high-quality and free services, with respect for the dignity and autonomy of every person".

The centres will also coordinate with local health and social care services.

The new centres will be launched across Greece, with particular emphasis on strengthening regional coverage and reducing inequalities in access to specialised mental health services.

A total of €28 million from ΕΣΠΑ 2021-2027 – Greece's main partnership agreement with the European Union – is planned for the creation and operation of the 20 new units. The budget amounts to €1.4 million per centre and covers the operation of both the day centre and the corresponding mobile unit for two years.

Good morning. Leo Cendrowicz here with your Thursday newsletter. We have almighty punch-up on our agenda today, as EU leaders gather in Brussels to brawl over their seven-year budget – a slugfest that almost certainly won’t be resolved by the end of the summit.

Brace yourselves. EU leaders gather in Brussels this morning for what promises to be one of the angriest summits in years. There is precious little goodwill in the room, no obvious broker capable of bridging the differences and virtually no expectation of a breakthrough. The meeting could spill into tomorrow, although it is hard to see what another night of haggling might achieve.

As Jorge Liboreiro reports, two of the EU’s most divisive issues are heading for a collision: the next seven-year budget and the financing of Ukraine’s war effort. Technically separate, they have become politically intertwined. And nothing brings out the worst in European solidarity quite like an argument about money.

Nobody’s happy. European Council President António Costa has lopped €204 billion off the Commission’s original €2 trillion budget proposal for 2028-2034. His reward? Complaints from virtually every corner of Europe.

The German-led frugals, who now prefer to call themselves the “modernisers”, want deeper cuts to agricultural subsidies and regional development funds, prioritising defence, technology and competitiveness instead. The 17 Friends of Cohesion, predominantly southern and eastern countries, think the cuts have already gone too far.

France, despite securing concessions on farming subsidies and a proposed digital tax, is also deeply unimpressed. Paris wants to preserve spending while avoiding an increase in its national contribution – a particularly tricky equation given the parlous state of French public finances.

The elephant in the room. Marine Le Pen is not attending the summit, but her presence will be felt. The far-right frontrunner in next spring’s French presidential election has threatened to slash France’s contribution to the EU budget. Emmanuel Macron insists negotiations cannot extend beyond December. Unfortunately, imposing a deadline is rather easier than meeting it.

Enter Ukraine. Russia’s relentless attacks have left Kyiv facing a €70 billion budget shortfall next year. The Commission is proposing another €45 billion loan, financed through joint borrowing, but Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria and the Czech Republic want no part in it.

An exasperated Friedrich Merz is threatening to veto the entire EU budget unless all 27 countries agree to support Ukraine. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico calls it a “textbook case of blackmail”.

The Commission’s suggested escape route would allow reluctant countries to contribute to the €20 billion earmarked for Ukraine’s civilian needs without participating in the €25 billion military component.

Guns versus butter. One of the more alarming aspects of the budget wrangling is that, for all the grand rhetoric about European sovereignty and military readiness, defence spending is also taking a hit. EU Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius warns that the proposed €39 billion cut to defence and space funding – a reduction of 30% – would jeopardise crucial pan-European programmes.

Former Commission President José Manuel Barroso weighed in, pointing to the glaring contradiction between European leaders’ declarations on defence and their willingness to pay for it. With Russia still waging war in Ukraine and Donald Trump proving an increasingly unreliable ally, the timing could hardly be worse.

Something to agree on? Leaders will also discuss Christine Lagarde’s successor at the European Central Bank, with Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos emerging as the favourite.

But the real measure of success by tomorrow will be whether a budget deal in December looks remotely achievable. The danger is that everyone leaves Brussels even angrier than when they arrived.

Meanwhile, the European Parliament is up in arms over Costa's proposed 10% cut to the MFF, threatening to reject the deal if it is struck by EU leaders. Vincenzo Genovese has the story from Strasbourg.

For more on this, follow our live blog on the EU summit.

In other news

With friends like these. So much for transatlantic trade peace. Donald Trump is proposing another round of tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including the EU, ostensibly to combat industrial overcapacity. European goods could face duties of 15% on top of existing most-favoured-nation tariffs, potentially rising to 20%. Brussels strongly rejects Washington’s premise, pointing out that Europe is itself a victim of global overcapacity. For Europeans who thought last year’s painstakingly negotiated trade deal offered some protection against Trump’s tariff whims, it’s another rude awakening.

Who picks up the tab? As EU leaders haggle over the next seven-year budget, Luca Bertuzzi and Kamuran Samar have put together a brilliant explainer on who would actually pay the proposed new EU taxes, complete with illuminating charts. The package could raise €60 billion annually, with Germany shouldering the biggest bill. Electronic waste, rather than Big Tech or tobacco, is the biggest money-spinner. Essential reading for understanding the national interests behind the budget horse-trading.

New faces, old dilemmas. Serbia’s absence from yesterday’s EU-Western Balkans summit has postponed a crucial test of its new leadership. The student movement that ousted Aleksandar Vučić is making encouraging noises about democratic reforms but remains decidedly coy about aligning with EU foreign policy. Sanctioning Russia, a move opposed by 67% of Serbians, and normalising relations with Kosovo remain particularly thorny issues. Brussels is still waiting to see whether Belgrade’s geopolitical compass has shifted.

Trouble in the marriage. The European Parliament’s Socialists and Liberals have suspended coalition talks with the centre-right EPP after it once again teamed up with the far right, this time to water down environmental safeguards, Vincenzo Genovese reports. They want written guarantees that Manfred Weber’s group will stop flirting with parties further to its right. Among the potential casualties of the spat: Roberta Metsola’s re-election as European Parliament president in January.

Taxing times. Brussels could slap a windfall tax on oil and gas giants without giving national governments a veto. A new legal study suggests the EU could sidestep unanimity rules if the levy genuinely serves climate or energy policy rather than simply raising revenue. With fuel prices soaring, fossil fuel companies enjoying bumper profits and EU leaders squabbling over the next budget, the timing is particularly intriguing.

Quantum leap. Having largely missed the boat on AI, Brussels is determined not to lose the next technology race. The Commission unveiled its Quantum Act yesterday, alongside a new fund designed to mobilise €50 billion in investment across critical technologies. Europe has a strong scientific pedigree in quantum but struggles to turn research into commercial success. There’s also a looming headache: quantum computers could crack today’s encryption systems.

Membership with strings attached. Getting into the EU is hard enough, but Montenegro could find itself under special scrutiny even after joining. The Commission wants to extend its monitoring of reforms beyond accession, alongside a 10-year probation period during which serious breaches of EU values could trigger the suspension of voting rights. It’s all designed to prevent another Viktor Orbán, although some member states question whether Brussels really needs another policing mechanism.

Follow the powder. Brussels wants to establish whether Irish-made alumina is feeding Russia’s war machine. Rather than banning exports of the raw material used to make aluminium, the Commission is proposing a reporting mechanism to track shipments to their final destination. Kyiv is disappointed, while Dublin fears hundreds of jobs could be at stake. An Irish investigation over the summer failed to settle the matter.

Political ippon? French judo legend turned presidential hopeful Teddy Riner has questioned France’s military support for Ukraine, saying that he did "not understand" why France was sending troops there. The five-time Olympic gold medallist asked whether Ukraine was even in the EU. Riner is currently polling at a modest 4.5%.

The inventory of Antoni Gaudí's estate reveals that the legendary Spanish architect wished to devote all his assets, including his Parc Güell house and his savings, to financing the works of the iconic Sagrada Família.

The inventory of Antoni Gaudí's estate has been revealed a century after his death and it shows the architect's deep committment to the Sagrada Familia. His last wish was to dedicate all his assets, from his savings to his home in Parc Güell, to financing the construction of the temple.

The document, kept in the Arxiu Històric de Protocols de Barcelona, is a 1926 copy of the will that Gaudí signed in 1911 in Puigcerdà. The original disappeared in 1936, after the notary's office that held it burned down in the first months of the Civil War. Among the papers is also the certificate of last wills signed by Manuel Azaña, then a Justice official and future president of the Second Republic.

As the dean of the Col·legi Notarial de Catalunya, José Alberto Marín, has explained, notarial documents are subject to protocol secrecy, but they are considered historical records and become open to public consultation once 100 years have passed.

An inheritance in the service of the Sagrada Familia

The inventory makes it possible to identify the three trusted heirs appointed by Gaudí, a figure specific to Catalan succession law. They were the priest Gil Parés i Vilasau, chaplain custodian of the Sagrada Familia; the doctor Pere Santaló i Castellví, a close friend of the architect; and Domènec Sugrañes i Gras, an architect and Gaudí's disciple who would later take over the direction of the works on the temple.

The three appeared before notary Luis Rufasta and recorded that Gaudí's express wish was to sell all his assets and hand over the money raised to the construction of the basilica. Sugrañes acted in place of Francesc Berenguer i Mestres, a close collaborator of the architect who had died in 1914.

A modest fortune and a single property

The inventory shows the austerity with which Gaudí lived in his final years. His savings were split between two bank accounts: one with 1,870 pesetas at the Banco de España in Barcelona, and another with 1,121 pesetas in a savings book at Caixa de Pensions per a la Vellesa i d'Estalvis.

His only property was the house in Parc Güell, in the former municipality of Gràcia, which the executors valued at 45,000 pesetas for the purposes of a possible sale. According to estimates by the Col·legi Notarial de Catalunya, that sum would be equivalent today to around €150,000 and represented an ordinary level of wealth for the time.

The documents confirm Gaudí's limited attachment to material possessions and his determination to put all his resources at the service of the project to which he devoted much of his life.

A document of particular historical value

The significance of the inventory goes beyond its financial content. The destruction of the original will in 1936 made this copy a key piece for reconstructing the architect's last wishes. In addition, the presence of Manuel Azaña's signature gives the document an element of particular historical interest.

After the legal period of 100 years has elapsed, the inventory will be available for consultation at the premises of the Col·legi Notarial de Catalunya, which has so far kept it in the Arxiu Històric de Protocols de Barcelona.

The archive also holds other documents linked to Gaudí and the Sagrada Familia, including the record of the laying of the basilica's first stone, signed before the architect took over the direction of the works.

Among its most recent holdings is also the document signed in June this year by the Pope Leo XIV and the Archbishop of Barcelona, Joan Josep Omella, which records the completion of the Tower of Jesus and the state of the works on the temple.

According to global property consultancy Colliers' 2027 report, Madrid, Lisbon and Barcelona rank among the ten European cities most sought after by property investors, as people in Spain and Portugal protest over the cost of housing.

EU leaders are set to clash over the next EU budget and future support for Ukraine at a crucial summit in Brussels.

The stage is set for a tense summit in Brussels where EU leaders will spar over the size of the next budget and future support for Ukraine.

On the table are two proposals.

The first, by European Council President António Costa, is a seven-year budget worth almost €1.7 trillion, which some leaders say is too much and others say is too little.

The second, by the European Commission, is a €45 billion support loan for Ukraine, financed through joint debt. Three countries – Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic – want to opt out of the loan, infuriating Kyiv's bilateral donors.

Although the budget and the loan are technically separate, they have become politically intertwined, creating a potentially volatile mix. After all, they are both about money.

"Now it's time for all of the leaders participating in this debate with an open mind, a constructive approach in the sense of compromise, because we need to approve this budget (by) the end of this year," Costa said on Thursday morning.

Also up for discussion is the succession of Christine Lagarde at the helm of the European Central Bank. Spain's candidate, Pablo Hernández de Cos, has taken the lead over Klaas Knot from the Netherlands and is widely tipped to snatch the top job.

Follow the Euronews live blog.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has criticised the European Commission's proposed package of sanctions against Russia, which, among other measures, targets Russian sports figures.

"We are going too far in politicising sporting and cultural events in this way,'" he said as he arrived at a European Council summit focused on support for Ukraine and the EU's next long-term budget.

The European Commission unveiled its latest sanctions package against Russia last Thursday, proposing to ban Russian sports teams and athletes competing under the Russian flag, as well as the display of official Russian symbols, from all sporting events inside the bloc.

It also wants to ban Russian nationals from making financial donations to, or holding positions within, governing bodies of European-based sports federations.

"Sports events can not be a forum for propaganda activities," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said last week when unveiling the latest package — the 22nd since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Brussels aims for a deal on the latest sanctions package in December before the Christmas break.

Who pays the EU’s new taxes?

European leaders are discussing a mix of new EU taxes, known as own resources, to finance the bloc’s next seven-year budget. They include measures involving electronic waste, unrecycled plastic, digital levies, carbon markets and tobacco. But who is going to pay for them?

Euronews breaks down how much each new tax is going to yield in terms of revenues, and who is going to foot the bill.

Bulgaria will join Ukraine loan but not its military strand, Bulgarian PM says

"The Baltics need to get the support to get our economy up to speed, so we can allocate resources for defence."

Cohesion and supporting Ukraine are both about solidarity, Lithuania’s President says

“For me, both issues are a matter of solidarity. First, the solidarity with Ukraine and the second, solidarity within the European Union,” said the President of Lithuania, Gitanas Nausėda.

For the Lithuanian leader, Costa’s proposal on the EU budget is a very good starting point for the leaders’ discussion. Still, he criticised the cuts to the Connecting Europe facility, the funding program for infrastructural projects.
